limits: Tool overview only; deeper MLOps, LLMOps and DAG theory deferred to Chapter 11.
Does not define a feature store, nor justify at length pairing NoSQL with a vector DB; prompt monitoring defined only briefly.
Tool choices (Qdrant best trade-off, Comet easiest) are asserted without benchmarks.
Tool list and versions (Bedrock model list, Poetry 1.8.3) date from 2024; chapter suggests uv may replace Poetry.
practices: Pin Python with pyenv and a .python-version file so the project uses 3.11.8 locally only (Python ecosystem).
Use Poetry with pyproject.toml and poetry.lock to pin the full dependency tree and avoid 'works on my machine' issues (Poetry).
Put CLI commands in a task runner (Poe the Poet) as living documentation (Poe section).
Write modular one-purpose functions, decorate as ZenML @step and glue with @pipeline (ZenML orchestrator).
Keep domain logic in a separate module from orchestrator code to avoid lock-in (ZenML orchestrator).
Attach precomputed metadata (size, splits, categories) to dataset artifacts for discovery (Artifacts and metadata).
Run pipelines from config files so inputs are tracked and reproducible (How to run and configure).
Log metrics, hyperparameters and system metrics in an experiment tracker (Comet ML).
Use specialised trace-based tools for prompt monitoring rather than plain logs (Opik).
Store raw unstructured data in a NoSQL DB, and processed data in a vector DB (Databases).
In production grant least-privilege IAM permissions; the book uses AdministratorAccess only for a test account (AWS setup).
Set billing alarms when following along on AWS (cost note).
